title: KAKE NEWS INVESTIGATES: Duplicate license plate numbers lead to dangerous situations for some Kansas drivers

reading.body:
This is a false positive in an automated identification system, produced because a partial identifier was treated as a unique one. Flock cameras read only letters and numbers, not plate backgrounds, so a specialty plate and a standard plate carrying the same number are indistinguishable to the system. Kansas issues the same number across more than 100 plate designs, which means the number alone does not identify a vehicle in that state. The system was operating in conditions it was not built to handle.

The failure sits at two points in the deployment. The first is the match between the camera reading and the stolen vehicle record, where a duplicated number and a wrong entry together produced an alert. The second is the officer's decision to act on that alert, which in one stop meant guns drawn and a driver handcuffed before the mistake was cleared. Catching it would have required the system to read plate backgrounds, or a human check of plate type against the record before a stop, or numbers that are not duplicated. Wichita police have discussed training Flock to recognize plate backgrounds, and the state's move to seven digit non duplicated numbers is described as the best solution.

What is not established is whether Flock was designed to distinguish plate types, or whether any officer or agency departed from policy. The account rests on a single outlet's investigation, and Capt. Casey Slaughter's statement that an alert alone is not enough to stop a car describes policy rather than a finding about these stops.

reports.title: KAKE NEWS INVESTIGATES: Duplicate license plate numbers lead to dangerous situations for some Kansas drivers

summary:
Kansas is moving from six digit license plate numbers to seven digit numbers because the state duplicates numbers across more than 100 plate designs. Matthew and Leah Spurlock have a KU Alumni plate numbered 7007. A stolen GMC pickup had a temporary Kansas tag with the same number, so Flock cameras alerted police. Colwich officers stopped the Spurlocks, then learned the wrong plate type had been entered. Later, Catoosa, Oklahoma police stopped them again after another Flock alert, drawing guns and handcuffing Matthew before the mistake was cleared up.

Wichita police Capt. Casey Slaughter said Flock cameras read only letters and numbers, not plate backgrounds, so they cannot tell specialty plates apart. He said a Flock alert alone is not enough to stop a car, but a wrong stolen vehicle entry can force officers to proceed. Wichita police have discussed training Flock to recognize plate backgrounds. The new seven digit, non duplicated numbers are the best solution. The Spurlocks' stolen plate entry has expired, so they no longer expect stops, and they hope to keep their 7007 KU tag.
